analysis.one_liner: Lets police officers be sued for civil rights violations by ending qualified immunity.
analysis.headline: A single House member introduced the bill with no cosponsors, and it has sat in the Judiciary Committee since January 2026 without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it much harder for police officers to escape civil lawsuits after violating someone's constitutional rights. Under the long-standing doctrine of qualified immunity, an officer can avoid liability unless the victim can show the exact right was 'clearly established' in prior court cases — a bar that has let many cases be thrown out. This bill would eliminate that defense for local and federal law enforcement officers. It would also loosen the criminal standard under 18 U.S.C. 242, the federal statute against depriving someone of their rights, so an officer could be convicted for 'knowingly or recklessly' causing a rights violation rather than 'willfully,' and it would make it easier to link an officer's conduct to a death.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of police misconduct and their families, who would gain a realistic path to sue officers in federal court and recover damages instead of watching cases dismissed because no prior case established the exact right at issue. Communities affected by police violence would also gain more accountability, since officers could no longer claim they acted in good faith or that the law was unsettled.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the qualified immunity defense — the argument that an officer acted in good faith or that the constitutional right was not 'clearly established' — from lawsuits under 42 U.S.C. 1983 against local law enforcement officers and from any legal action against federal law enforcement officers [S2].

It lowers the criminal intent standard in 18 U.S.C. 242 from 'willfully' to 'knowingly or recklessly,' making federal criminal charges for deprivation of rights easier to prove, and it defines death as resulting from an act that was a 'substantial factor contributing to' the death [S2].
It removes the death penalty from the list of possible sentences under that criminal statute [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement officers, who would face personal civil liability without the good-faith defense; and local governments and their taxpayers, who would bear higher settlement, judgment, and liability-insurance costs as more suits survive dismissal. Federal and local law enforcement agencies would also face more criminal exposure for officers' conduct.

drawbacks.text: Lowering the criminal standard from 'willfully' to 'knowingly or recklessly' means officers could face federal charges for split-second judgment calls that a jury later deems reckless, and eliminating the good-faith defense removes the protection for officers who made an honest mistake about an unclear law — the exact situations qualified immunity was designed to cover [S2].
The added 'substantial factor' causation rule for deaths could broaden liability well beyond the officer whose conduct was the direct cause of a death [S2].

Higher civil liability against local police would be paid in significant part by municipal budgets and insurance premiums — that is, by local taxpayers — not only by the individual officers sued [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly targets the main procedural obstacle — qualified immunity — that has prevented victims of police misconduct from getting compensation, and it does so by statute, which is the only way to override a judicially created doctrine. The costs are real but the trade-off is deliberate: officers and governments would face more suits, and courts would sort legitimate claims from weak ones. Removing the death penalty from the criminal statute while easing the intent standard blunts some criticism that the bill is purely punitive, though opponents of any qualified-immunity elimination would still call it unfair to officers making good-faith errors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in January 2026 and has sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and no other member has signed on.

narrative.text: Rep. Julie Johnson of Texas introduced the bill on January 30, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S4].
The only action since referral is the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on February 4, 2026 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the outcome is unchanged for everyone: officers and governments still have qualified immunity because the bill has not advanced. The bill's sponsor benefits only from having introduced it for the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: police keep immunity for now

for.name: Rep. Julie Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor on February 4, 2026.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over civil rights and criminal law
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — since it was referred on January 30, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has only a Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and no vote has ever been taken, so there is no record of how the parties line up.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill strips away qualified immunity, the doctrine that has shielded officers from most civil rights lawsuits, and eases the criminal standard for officers whose conduct causes a rights violation. Police unions have historically opposed any elimination of qualified immunity, which is central to officers' personal legal protection.

Local governments would face more surviving lawsuits and higher settlements and insurance costs, which fall partly on taxpayers. Governments lose money under the bill, though that exposure is the accountability mechanism the bill creates for the public.
More civil suits surviving dismissal would mean more premiums for insurers that cover police departments, though possibly also larger payouts.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action more than a month after introduction, the bill is all but certain to die in the House Judiciary Committee at the end of this Congress. Its closest precedent, the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act, which the bill's text borrows definitions from, passed the House in earlier Congresses but never became law; a one-sponsor bill with no cosponsors has far less support than that.
